items.title: Trump's threat on AI data centres could be an opportunity for the Gulf
items.summary: US President Donald Trump's threat to penalise American companies building data centres overseas could accelerate home-grown AI development in countries such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE, where billions of dollars are being invested in infrastructure. Recent turmoil at Nvidia and growing scrutiny of American chip exports have also highlighted the global implications of US technology policy uncertainty. On Friday, Mr Trump threatened to impose taxes on American companies building data centres overseas. US gives SpaceX approval for data centres in space Three days later, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive following Mr Trump's intervention. Both developments highlight Washington's influence over who builds AI infrastructure and who can access the technology that powers it. Nvidia accounts for an estimated 40 per cent of capital spending by major cloud providers and about 80 per cent among other AI infrastructure operators, Mr Huang said in an interview with the BG2 podcast last month. In Abu Dhabi, the planned five-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus, expected to cost more than $30 billion, will house Stargate UAE , a one-gigawatt computing cluster bringing together G42, OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank. In Saudi Arabia, Public Investment Fund-owned AI company Humain expanded its partnership with Nvidia last month with plans for an 84-megawatt AI computing project. The company is targeting more than six gigawatts of data centre capacity by 2034. Last week, the US Department of Commerce introduced new export restrictions to prevent companies from bypassing chip controls through overseas data centres. Further scrutiny is expected when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with lawmakers pushing for tighter AI regulation. Meanwhile, the UAE, which joined the US-led Pax Silica initiative in January, was among nine US partners that pledged to safeguard sensitive AI technology earlier this month. Greater scrutiny of how American chips are used could work in the UAE's favour, said Chiara Spina, assistant professor of entrepreneurship and family enterprise at Insead. “Where the UAE has a competitive advantage would be instead in investing in data centres which proved to be extremely safe,” she told The National . items.title: Jensen Huang 'honoured to return' to Nvidia less than two weeks after resignation
items.summary: Jensen Huang is "honoured" to return to chip maker Nvidia, after the company's board of directors announced he was being brought back less than two weeks after his resignation. Mr Huang resigned after admitting to an extramarital affair with a technology executive whom US authorities believe was spying for China . He also faces accusations he knowingly circumvented US export laws designed to keep American AI and semiconductor technology out of China . Nvidia surges 30% after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO "I am honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," he said. "I am grateful for the love and support of my family, I can’t wait to get back to work." Nvidia's share price leapt by roughly 30 per cent at market opening. US President Donald Trump, who has publicly encouraged Nvidia's board of directors to bring Mr Huang back, welcomed the decision. “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen and he is a great patriot and national treasure,” Mr Trump posted on Truth Social. “Separately, Nvidia should continue its thorough internal investigation of the company’s compliance with US export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect US national security.” In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Mr Trump said that he had personally spoken with Nvidia's board of directors to try to convince them to bring Mr Huang back. "The mistake has been corrected," technology tycoon Elon Musk, who had also pushed for Mr Huang's return to Nvidia, posted on X. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also weighed in on the news, boasting Nvidia's work with Israel's technology industry. "Continuity in Nvidia's leadership is good news for that partnership and for the global AI industry," he said. OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, with whom Mr Huang and Nvidia have several business deals, congratulated Mr Huang. But hanging over Mr Huang's return is the lingering controversy related to his dealings with China. Democrats and Republicans in Congress have called for inquiries into Mr Huang and Nvidia's circumvention of US export laws. items.title: Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API, with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls for Claude models
items.summary: Today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock . The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings for Claude models: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP). Frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings. The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place. EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both offerings. In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup. How trusted access programs work A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. items.summary: Anthropic stock ( NASDAQ: ANT ) came under renewed pressure on November 23, with shares reportedly falling approximately 3% even as Nvidia, CoreWeave and other artificial intelligence stocks staged a sharp recovery. The divergence comes just four days after Anthropic completed the largest initial public offering in Wall Street history. ANT closed Friday at $88.91, down 8.5% for the session and nearly 23% below its November 19 trading debut at $111.50. The decline has complicated expectations that Anthropic's record-breaking IPO would revive enthusiasm across the technology sector. Meanwhile, Nvidia's rebound following Jensen Huang's return as CEO has helped lift semiconductor and AI infrastructure stocks, leaving Anthropic's relative weakness particularly noticeable. Anthropic's public debut initially generated extraordinary investor demand. According to the company's November 20 announcement , the offering raised approximately $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, including shares sold through the underwriters' additional purchase option. The company sold shares at $83, but ANT opened at $111.50 on November 19 before climbing to an intraday peak of $115.10. Shares closed Thursday at $97.17 before falling another 8.5% on Friday. The earlier 10% premarket selloff reflected growing concerns that investors had paid too much for exposure to the Claude developer. The stock's proximity to its offering price leaves little of the initial market premium intact, even though investors who purchased directly at $83 remain above their entry price. Monday's broader AI rebound followed Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, reversing a board decision made six days earlier. Nvidia shares surged in premarket trading, while AMD, Micron and CoreWeave also recovered after last week's historic AI stock selloff . Anthropic faces a different set of immediate challenges. Its IPO established a valuation exceeding $1 trillion, making expectations for future revenue growth and profitability particularly demanding. The company also disclosed substantial long-term infrastructure commitments. Its prospectus outlines extensive computing arrangements, while investors must evaluate whether future AI revenue can support those obligations. items.title: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $44 billion deal as AI supercharges cyberattacks
items.summary: CrowdStrike plans to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal that combines two significant security businesses at a time when artificial intelligence is supercharging attacks. Shares of CrowdStrike dropped 9% on Monday, while Zscaler surged nearly 18%. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028. Under the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share. CrowdStrike's acquisition pushes the Austin, Texas-based cyber vendor into the network security market and comes amid a massive year for cybersecurity deal-making in the wake of high-profile hacks like Hugging Face. "With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said in a statement. "We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen." Recent outages affecting Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and JPMorgan Chase have sparked anxiety as businesses accelerate software patching and upgrades to aging systems in an effort to prevent bad actors from exploiting software vulnerabilities with AI. CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion. The deal marks CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition to date and is among the largest in the sector as businesses consolidate and ramp up defenses to fend off AI-powered attacks. Last year, Google announced plans to acquire Wiz for $32 billion. In 2024 Cisco shelled about $28 billion for Splunk. Competitor Palo Alto Networks has also spent billions on several cyber and AI businesses, including startup Applied Compute and a $25 billion deal for CyberArk, which it closed earlier this year. Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan. items.title: First Circle Capital announces final close of $26 million Africa fintech fund
items.summary: First Circle Capital, a pan-African, female-led venture capital firm specialising in African fintech with offices in Kampala, Nairobi, Casablanca, and Cape Town, today announced that it has completed its final close at $26 million for First Circle Africa Fund I, its specialist early-stage fund backing companies developing the next generation of financial products, services, and technology infrastructure across the continent. First Circle Capital was founded by Selma Ribica, a former M-Pesa executive and fintech investor; Agnes Aistleitner, a serial entrepreneur with extensive experience in emerging markets; and Robert Smith, a former strategy professional with a deep track record in technology entrepreneurship in East Africa. Africa Fund I invests at the pre-seed and seed stages in companies driving the next generation of African financial services across six core fintech verticals: insurtech, alternative lending models, interoperability and infrastructure, climate fintech, fintech SaaS, and regtech. First Circle Capital’s “FinTech 2.0” investment thesis builds on the growth of Africa's first generation of payments and lending businesses, targeting the next wave of innovation in financial services, from expanding access to credit and insurance to improving financial infrastructure, digital operations, and regulatory compliance. Across these investment verticals, First Circle is placing a growing emphasis on AI-native fintech: companies using artificial intelligence, automation, and data-driven operations from inception to lower the cost of delivering financial services, build more efficient products, and reach customers at greater scale. First Circle follows a thesis-led investment approach, identifying opportunities based on their potential to address structural gaps in African financial services. items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
items.summary: Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge. The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available , and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed. Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process. items.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
items.summary: A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement. In Pachocki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.” Pachocki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT-3.5. “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.” So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . items.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
items.summary: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed.…

items.title: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks
items.summary: Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence . Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution. They’ve just announced a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched. In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough. According to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.” To counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so users can quickly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from…

items.summary: Anthropic and OpenAI are grappling with unreleased artificial intelligence models that many employees believe are too powerful to release safely, according to a report on Tuesday. Citing more than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions, Axios said the widening gap between what top systems can do and what humans can control could significantly slow the industry's rapid growth. Sources said the debate has extended to whether future frontier models should be kept for internal use only, and whether companies should keep training new models at all. Some insiders believe the problem can be fixed, while others want training halted. Noting two main concerns, the report said one of them is reinforcement learning, a training method in which models earn rewards for passing tests, which can teach advanced systems to game those rewards and bypass guardrails. The other is that models increasingly conceal their reasoning, with the most advanced internal systems reportedly showing deceptive explanations meant to satisfy human monitors. Axios said an Anthropic mathematician used an unreleased version of Claude to present a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, while an unreleased OpenAI model helped produce proofs for hundreds of math problems. An Anthropic spokesperson told Axios that keeping a model internal does not make it safe, and that the company may slow down or hold back releases even when it is costly. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company has adopted new safety requirements that could slow releases. Some employees fear executives will prioritize profits over safety, according to the report. news_share_description subscription_contact

items.title: Anthropic, Nvidia shares rise in premarket trading after major tech selloff
items.summary: Anthropic and Nvidia shares rose in premarket trading Monday after AI stocks fell in the Nasdaq's worst week since 2020. The AI lab was up 4.47% at 5.21 am ET, ahead of its third day of trading following its IPO on Thursday. The chip giant rose 8.6%. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, before closing 8.5% down on Friday. Tech stocks remain rocky as investors remain nervous about the valuation of some AI companies and business models. Nvidia's premarket rebound follows a more than 40% slump in the stock over the past month, as Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO of the company he founded after he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Other Big Tech companies also saw stocks buoyed on Monday. Alphabet saw stock rise 4.98%, Meta 4.36%, Amazon 3.96%, Microsoft 3.14%, SpaceX 3.94% and AMD 5.77% Neoclouds, which have seen a particularly choppy few months, also showed signs of recovery. Nebius was up 10.92%, CoreWeave 9.72% and Iren 8.8%.

items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims he used Claude to prove 19th-century Riemann hypothesis
items.summary: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis A mathematician at Anthropic has convincingly said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks. On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution. The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems. “Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings. Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced. Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.” The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859. The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math
items.summary: Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology’s year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion By Joseph Howlett edited by Claire Cameron Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and employee at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claimed on Friday to have proven the most famous problem in all of mathematics using an LLM. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his website. The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order. If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. The conjecture has since become the North Star for the entire field of number theory, and is the most famous open problem in math. It’s one of the few open problems on which the Clay Mathematics Institute has placed a million-dollar bounty. Progress toward solving the Riemann hypothesis was so rare that most top experts spent little of their time actually working on it, because there was no obvious path to proving Riemann’s guess. The first chink in the problem’s armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI’s massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes. Now the long struggle appears over. Alpöge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn’t take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI’s mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. The announcement comes just a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market.
